newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 27.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents.
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- PARIS HIT BY SWING TO SOCIALISTS

The French franc fell against other currencies and share prices fell sharply on the Paris bourse on Monday, as markets reacted to the surprise election results showing a swing from the centre- right coalition to the socialists. While the CAC-40 stock market index fell almost four percent on the day, some stocks - notably banks, defence companies and privatisation stocks - lost more than 10 percent of their value.
-- BARCLAYS CALLS FOR HIGHER RATES

Economists at Barclays Bank are set to warn that inflation is building up and that interest rates may have to rise substantially. Barclays' economics director Chris Wright has forecast that inflation, currently 2.5 percent, will rise to 3.8 percent by next year. He urges chancellor Gordon Brown to take action now to avoid volatility in the economy in the coming years.
-- HALIFAX COUNTS THE SELLERS

The Halifax building society will reveal on Tuesday how many of its customers have opted to sell their shares in the company ahead of a planned floatation. The shares start trading on June 2, and some City analysts have suggested that the strong performance of other banking stocks makes it unlikely that the number of sellers will match the 27 percent of Alliance and Leicester investors who sold before floatation.
THE TIMES
-- CBI PUSHES FOR FULL PFI PARTNERSHIP

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI), formerly a fierce critic of the operation of the Private Finance Initiative (PFI), has said it would like to manage the policy as a partner. The PFI was set up to encourage private companies to fund public sector construction projects. However, the CBI is frustrated at huge delays and heavy administration which have built up, and is keen to tackle the problems and clear the logjam of projects.
-- OECD PRAISES BRITAIN OVER LABOUR REFORM

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has praised Britain's record for reducing structural unemployment over the past decade, but has attacked leading European countries that it believes are lagging behind in the introduction of vital labour market reforms. In a report prepared for the OECD's annual ministerial meeting, the organisation cites Britain along with the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Irish Republic as role models for improving labour market performance through wide-ranging structural reform.
-- LONDON TO LEAD EUROPE FOR ECONOMIC GROWTH

The annual report on European regional prospects compiled by the European Economic Research and Advisory Consortium (Ereco) has predicted that London's economy will grow at a faster rate than any of its major European rivals over the next five years, even if the UK stays outside a single currency. The consortium, a group of leading economic research institutes, claims that London will maintain its position as Europe's most important
financial centre.
THE GUARDIAN
-- WELFARE-TO-WORK WILL HELP EDUCATION FUNDING

The government is planning to use some of the estimated 90 billion stg savings from the social security budget, to be created by a strategy of taking people off benefits and putting them in work, to help fund the education system. Speaking at an OECD conference in Paris, Helen Liddell, Economic Secretary to the Treasury, said the government would concentrate its efforts on settling long-term unemployment but that a better-skilled workforce was essential for long-term prosperity.
-- CHANNEL 4 BROADCASTS PROFITS WARNING

Broadcaster Channel 4 has warned that its profits for 1997 are likely to be lower than the 134 million stg it reported for 1996. The company said that the era of rapidly rising advertising revenue, which began when it started selling its own airtime in 1993, has come to a halt. The warning, which could have implications for other broadcasters and advertising dependent media, is likely to kill-off speculation about the privatisation of Channel 4.
-- ZENECA MERGER TALK FADES AS ROCHE UNVEILS 6.5 BILLION STG DEAL

Swiss pharmaceuticals group Roche Holding AG has announced plans to invest 15 billion Swiss francs (6.5 billion stg) in building up its diagnostics expertise. The announcement dashed hopes that the Swiss company might merge with one of Britain's leading drugs firms, such as Zeneca. Shares in Zeneca have risen steadily over the past year, in part due to merger speculation, although the company has always denied it has entered any talks about a deal.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- DISCLOSURE RIFT HAMPERS FORMULA ONE SELL-OFF

The planned two billion stg floatation of the Formula One motor racing business is currently stalled on the starting grid as advisers to the sale remain locked in negotiations with the stock exchange. The sticking point appears to be the level of financial disclosure in the prospectus for potential investors, and in particular how much detail should appear of the organisation's exclusive Grand Prix television rights.
-- QUANTUM ENERGY TO BUY VECTOR GAS

London-based gas company Quantum Energy Group is set to announce an agreement to purchase Vector Gas, a joint-venture company between Scottish Hydro-Electric and Marathon Oil of the US. The acquisition, for an undisclosed sum, takes Quantum's combined operations to some two percent of the UK industrial and commercial gas market.
-- GERMAN MINISTERS FALL OUT OVER EMU

German finance minister Theo Waigel is continuing to suffer fall-out over the country's difficulties in meeting Emu qualification criteria. Guenter Rexrodt, Germany's economics minister, has criticised Waigel in a row over economic forecasts. Rexrodt was responding to claims by Waigel that other government departments had botched economic forecasts and left him searching for billions of marks to cut Bonn's budget deficit in order to meet Emu convergence targets.
